entities.name: Demolition of Masjid al-Dirar
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Demolition of Masjid al-Dirar (Arabic: مسجد الضرار, the Mosque of Harm/Dissension) is one of the most significant events in early Islamic history, recorded in the Quran (Surah At-Tawbah 9:107-110): during the Prophet Muhammad's return from the Tabuk expedition (630 CE), a group of hypocrites (munafiqun) in Medina had built a second mosque at Dhuba, near the original Quba Mosque, ostensibly for worship but actually (according to the Quran's account) for divisive purposes and to serve as a base for an enemy agent named Abu Amir al-Rahib. The Prophet Muhammad ordered the mosque demolished.

The Quran's verses about Masjid al-Dirar establish the theological principle that a mosque built for harmful or divisive purposes rather than genuine worship is not a legitimate place of worship and should not be prayed in. This principle has been cited in Islamic jurisprudence for 1,400 years in discussions of mosque legitimacy, the conditions for valid mosque founding, and the distinction between genuine Islamic worship and weaponized religious institutions.

The event carries exceptional theological weight in Islamic tradition: it is one of the very few historical events explicitly addressed and condemned in the Quran itself, establishing a precedent that even a physical mosque building is not automatically sacred or legitimate if founded for wrong purposes. This theological-jurisprudential principle has been applied in many subsequent contexts, including contemporary debates about mosques used for radical recruitment and similar situations.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Demolition of Masjid al-Dirar — one of the few historical events directly addressed and condemned in the Quran, establishing the principle of mosque legitimacy in Islamic jurisprudence — is historically significant as a foundational event in early Islamic theological-legal tradition with 1,400 years of jurisprudential application.
